title: The Symmetric Perceptron: a Teacher-Student Scenario
summary: We introduce and solve a teacher-student formulation of the symmetric binary Perceptron, turning a traditionally storage-oriented model into a planted inference problem with a guaranteed solution at any sample density. We adapt the formulation of the symmetric Perceptron which traditionally considers either the u-shaped potential or the rectangular one, by including labels in both regions. With this formulation, we analyze both the Bayes-optimal regime at for noise-less examples and the effect of thermal noise under two different potential/classification rules. Using annealed and quenched free-entropy calculations in the high-dimensional limit, we map the phase diagram in the three control parameters, namely the sample density $α$, the distance between the origin and one of the symmetric hyperplanes $κ$ and temperature $T$, and identify a robust scenario where learning is organized by a second-order instability that creates teacher-correlated suboptimal states, followed by a first-order transition to full alignment. We show how this structure depends on the choice of potential, the interplay between metastability of the suboptimal solution and its melting towards the planted configuration, which is relevant for Monte Carlo-based optimization algorithms.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a teacher-student formulation of the symmetric binary Perceptron, transforming it from a storage model to a planted inference problem with guaranteed solutions at any sample density, and analyzes its phase diagram using statistical physics methods.
AI.motivation: To transform the traditional storage-oriented symmetric binary Perceptron model into a planted inference problem with guaranteed solutions, enabling analysis of learning dynamics and phase transitions in high-dimensional settings.
AI.method: Adapt the symmetric Perceptron formulation by including labels in both regions, analyze Bayes-optimal regime for noise-less examples and thermal noise effects under two potential/classification rules, using annealed and quenched free-entropy calculations in high-dimensional limit.
AI.result: Mapped phase diagram in three control parameters (sample density α, distance κ, temperature T), identified robust scenario with second-order instability creating teacher-correlated suboptimal states followed by first-order transition to full alignment, showing dependence on potential choice and interplay between metastability and melting.
AI.conclusion: The teacher-student formulation reveals rich phase structure with distinct learning regimes, providing insights into optimization algorithms and the fundamental limits of learning in symmetric binary Perceptrons, with implications for Monte Carlo-based optimization.

title: The Born Rule as the Unique Refinement-Stable Induced Weight on Robust Record Sectors
comment: Quantum foundations. Distinct conditional uniqueness theorem for induced weight on robust record sectors
summary: This paper proves a conditional structural uniqueness theorem for induced weight on robust record sectors within an admissible Hilbert record layer. Its theorem target and additive carrier differ from those of the standard Born-rule routes: additivity is not placed on the full projector lattice, but on disjoint admissible continuation bundles through an extensive bundle valuation, from which the sector-level additive law is inherited under admissible refinement. Accordingly, the result is not a Gleason-type representation theorem in different language, but a distinct uniqueness theorem about induced sector weight inherited from bundle additivity on admissible continuation structure. Under two explicit structural conditions, internal equivalence of admissible binary refinement profiles and sufficient admissible refinement richness, the quadratic assignment is the only non-negative refinement-stable induced weight on robust record sectors. In the main theorem, refinement richness is secured by admissible binary saturation. A supplementary proposition shows that dense admissible saturation already suffices if continuity of the profile function is added. Under normalization, the result reduces to the standard Born assignment.

AI.tldr: Conditional uniqueness theorem for induced weight on robust record sectors in admissible Hilbert record layers, showing Born rule is the only non-negative refinement-stable weight under specific structural conditions.
AI.motivation: To establish a distinct uniqueness theorem for induced sector weight that differs from standard Gleason-type representation theorems, focusing on weight inherited from bundle additivity on admissible continuation structures rather than full projector lattice additivity.
AI.method: Proves conditional structural uniqueness theorem using extensive bundle valuation on disjoint admissible continuation bundles, with sector-level additive law inherited under admissible refinement. Requires two explicit structural conditions: internal equivalence of admissible binary refinement profiles and sufficient admissible refinement richness.
AI.result: Under specified conditions, the quadratic assignment (Born rule) is the only non-negative refinement-stable induced weight on robust record sectors. Main theorem uses admissible binary saturation for refinement richness; supplementary proposition shows dense admissible saturation suffices with continuity of profile function.
AI.conclusion: The paper establishes a distinct uniqueness theorem for induced sector weight that reduces to the standard Born assignment under normalization, providing a conditional structural foundation for quantum probability assignments based on admissible continuation bundle structure.

title: Implementing non-Abelian Hatano-Nelson model in electric circuits
summary: Non-Hermitian systems generally host complex spectra that bring unique spectral topologies, leading to the spectral braiding and non-Hermitian skin effect. The experimental exploration of non-Hermitian physics is mainly concentrated in artificial systems due to the flexibility in the introduction of the non-Hermiticity, but to date has focused only on the systems without gauge fields or with Abelian gauge fields. Here, we propose a non-Abelian Hatano-Nelson model with a nonreciprocal U(2) gauge field. The gauge field induces two non-Hermitian phenomena: the first is the Hopf-link-shaped complex energy braiding, and the second is the bipolar skin effect arising under the non-Abelian condition. The non-Abelian Hatano-Nelson model is implemented in electric circuits, and the Hopf-link-shaped admittance spectra and bipolar skin admittance modes are observed. Our work enriches the experimental non-Hermitian physics, and provides an approach to designing multifunctional non-Hermitian devices.

AI.tldr: Experimental realization of a non-Abelian Hatano-Nelson model with U(2) gauge field in electric circuits, demonstrating Hopf-link energy braiding and bipolar skin effect.
AI.motivation: Non-Hermitian systems offer unique spectral topologies and phenomena like spectral braiding and skin effects, but experimental exploration has been limited to systems without gauge fields or with only Abelian gauge fields. There's a need to explore non-Abelian gauge fields in non-Hermitian systems.
AI.method: Proposed a non-Abelian Hatano-Nelson model with a nonreciprocal U(2) gauge field. Implemented this model experimentally using electric circuits to observe the predicted phenomena.
AI.result: Successfully observed two key phenomena: 1) Hopf-link-shaped complex energy braiding in admittance spectra, and 2) bipolar skin admittance modes arising from the non-Abelian condition. The experimental results confirm theoretical predictions.
AI.conclusion: This work enriches experimental non-Hermitian physics by extending it to non-Abelian gauge fields, and provides a practical approach for designing multifunctional non-Hermitian devices using electric circuits.

title: Spectral methods: crucial for machine learning, natural for quantum computers?
summary: This article presents an argument for why quantum computers could unlock new methods for machine learning. We argue that spectral methods, in particular those that learn, regularise, or otherwise manipulate the Fourier spectrum of a machine learning model, are often natural for quantum computers. For example, if a generative machine learning model is represented by a quantum state, the Quantum Fourier Transform allows us to manipulate the Fourier spectrum of the state using the entire toolbox of quantum routines, an operation that is usually prohibitive for classical models. At the same time, spectral methods are surprisingly fundamental to machine learning: A spectral bias has recently been hypothesised to be the core principle behind the success of deep learning; support vector machines have been known for decades to regularise in Fourier space, and convolutional neural nets build filters in the Fourier space of images. Could, then, quantum computing open fundamentally different, much more direct and resource-efficient ways to design the spectral properties of a model? We discuss this potential in detail here, hoping to stimulate a direction in quantum machine learning research that puts the question of ``why quantum?'' first.

AI.tldr: Quantum computers could enable novel machine learning approaches by naturally implementing spectral methods that manipulate Fourier spectra, which are fundamental to many classical ML techniques but computationally expensive.
AI.motivation: The paper argues that quantum computers may provide fundamentally different and more efficient ways to design spectral properties of machine learning models, addressing the core question of "why quantum?" for ML applications.
AI.method: The authors propose leveraging quantum computing's natural affinity for spectral methods, particularly through operations like the Quantum Fourier Transform, to manipulate Fourier spectra of models represented as quantum states.
AI.result: The paper presents a conceptual argument that quantum computers could enable direct manipulation of spectral properties that are prohibitive for classical models, potentially opening new avenues in machine learning design.
AI.conclusion: Quantum computing may offer fundamentally different, more direct and resource-efficient ways to design spectral properties of machine learning models, suggesting a promising research direction that prioritizes understanding "why quantum?" for ML.

title: A versatile neural-network toolbox for testing Bell locality in networks
comment: 10+4 pages, 4+3 figures, RevTeX 4.2. The computational appendix is available at https://www.github.com/Antoine0Girardin/local_model_in_networks
summary: Determining whether an observed distribution of events generated in a quantum network is Bell local, i.e., if it admits an alternative realization in terms of independent local variables, is extremely challenging. Building upon arXiv:1907.10552, we develop a software solution that parameterizes local models in networks via neural networks. This allows one to leverage optimization tools available from the machine learning community in the search of network Bell nonlocality. Our solution applies to arbitrary networks, is easy to use, and includes technical improvements that significantly increase performance compared to previous implementations. We apply it to investigate nonlocality in several networks hitherto unexplored, providing insights on the corresponding quantum nonlocal sets and suggesting concrete, promising realizations of quantum nonlocal correlations.

AI.tldr: Neural network-based software for detecting Bell nonlocality in quantum networks, applicable to arbitrary networks with improved performance over previous methods.
AI.motivation: The challenge of determining whether observed quantum network event distributions are Bell local (admit local variable explanations) is extremely difficult, requiring better computational tools.
AI.method: Develops software that parameterizes local models in quantum networks using neural networks, leveraging machine learning optimization tools to search for network Bell nonlocality.
AI.result: The solution applies to arbitrary networks, is easy to use, includes technical improvements that significantly increase performance compared to previous implementations, and has been applied to investigate nonlocality in several previously unexplored networks.
AI.conclusion: The neural network approach provides insights on quantum nonlocal sets and suggests concrete, promising realizations of quantum nonlocal correlations in network scenarios.

title: Inequality for Strong-Weak Spontaneous Symmetry Breaking in Fermionic Open Quantum systems
summary: Under decoherence, an initial Gaussian (free-fermion) state evolves into a non-Gaussian mixed state, so the resulting decohered fermionic state is not exactly solvable in general. We show through an inequality that a class of Rényi-2 correlators of the decohered fermion state are upper-bounded by the Rényi-2 correlator serving as a proximate diagnostic of strong-weak spontaneous symmetry breaking (SW-SSB) of the charge-U(1) symmetry. This inequality holds for arbitrary decoherence strength and suggests that decoherence drives fermionic quantum matter toward U(1) SW-SSB. We also make connections between our inequality and other subjects such as projected quantum spin Hall insulator and Dirac spin liquid states.

AI.tldr: Decoherence drives fermionic quantum matter toward U(1) strong-weak spontaneous symmetry breaking (SW-SSB), with Rényi-2 correlators of decohered states bounded by SW-SSB diagnostic correlators.
AI.motivation: To understand how decoherence affects fermionic quantum matter, particularly whether it drives systems toward specific symmetry-breaking phases, and to establish connections between decoherence phenomena and known quantum states.
AI.method: Develop an inequality showing that Rényi-2 correlators of decohered fermion states are upper-bounded by a Rényi-2 correlator serving as a diagnostic for U(1) strong-weak spontaneous symmetry breaking (SW-SSB), valid for arbitrary decoherence strength.
AI.result: The inequality demonstrates that decoherence drives fermionic quantum matter toward U(1) SW-SSB, and connections are established with projected quantum spin Hall insulator and Dirac spin liquid states.
AI.conclusion: Decoherence universally pushes fermionic systems toward U(1) strong-weak spontaneous symmetry breaking, providing a unifying framework connecting decoherence phenomena with various quantum phases of matter.

title: Multipartite entanglement dynamics in quantum walks
summary: Quantum walks constitute a rich area of quantum information science, where multipartite entanglement plays a central role in the dynamics and scalability of quantum advantage over classical simulators. In this work, we study the multipartite entanglement of quantum walks in optical settings. We present methods for computing a geometric measure of entanglement for arbitrary partitions of a single-walker quantum walk and for analyzing the entanglement in multi-walker scenarios. These techniques are used for numerical studies on the entanglement dynamics of quantum walks in large systems and under various initial conditions. For a given bipartition, based on the coin degrees of freedom, we derive exact expressions describing the complete entanglement dynamics for arbitrary localized initial conditions. We use these expressions for analytic statements about the asymptotic behavior of the system. Furthermore, we demonstrate the emergence of entanglement typicality in statistical ensembles of random optical networks.

AI.tldr: The paper studies multipartite entanglement in quantum walks using optical settings, developing methods to compute geometric entanglement measures and deriving exact expressions for entanglement dynamics.
AI.motivation: Multipartite entanglement is crucial for quantum walks' dynamics and scalability advantages over classical simulators, particularly in optical implementations where understanding entanglement properties is essential for quantum information applications.
AI.method: Developed methods for computing geometric entanglement measures for arbitrary partitions in single-walker quantum walks and analyzed multi-walker scenarios; derived exact expressions for complete entanglement dynamics based on coin degrees of freedom; used numerical studies on large systems and various initial conditions; demonstrated entanglement typicality in random optical networks.
AI.result: Exact expressions describing complete entanglement dynamics for arbitrary localized initial conditions; analytic statements about asymptotic behavior; demonstration of entanglement typicality in statistical ensembles of random optical networks; numerical studies on entanglement dynamics in large quantum walk systems.
AI.conclusion: The work provides comprehensive analytical and numerical tools for studying multipartite entanglement in quantum walks, enabling deeper understanding of entanglement dynamics, asymptotic behavior, and typicality in optical quantum walk implementations.

title: Phased outcome-complete simulation
summary: We generalize the polynomial-time outcome-complete simulation algorithm for stabilizer circuits in arXiv:2309.08676 to track global phases exactly, yielding what we call phased outcome-complete simulation. The original algorithm enabled equivalence checking of stabilizer circuits with intermediate measurements and conditional Pauli corrections for all input states and all measurement outcomes simultaneously, but it tracked quantum states only up to a global phase. Our generalization removes this limitation and enables equivalence checking for an important family of non-stabilizer circuits: stabilizer circuits augmented with single-qubit rotations $\exp(iαZ)$ by symbolic angles. Two such circuits are equivalent if they implement the same quantum channel for all values of the symbolic angles and all measurement outcomes, given a one-to-one correspondence between rotation angles in the two circuits and a mapping between measurement outcomes. This model enables testing of compilation algorithms that transform the Clifford portions of a computation while preserving rotation angles. Examples include Pauli-based computation, edge-disjoint path compilation for surface codes, and custom compilation strategies for reversible circuits such as adders, multipliers, and table lookups. Our efficient classical verification methods extend naturally to circuits with outcome-parity-conditional Pauli gates and intermediate measurements, features that are ubiquitous in fault-tolerant quantum computing but are rarely addressed by existing equivalence-checking approaches.

AI.tldr: Extends stabilizer circuit simulation to track global phases exactly, enabling equivalence checking for circuits with symbolic-angle rotations and measurement-dependent corrections.
AI.motivation: Existing stabilizer circuit simulation algorithms track quantum states only up to global phase, limiting their ability to verify equivalence for circuits containing non-stabilizer elements like symbolic-angle rotations. There's a need for verification methods that handle features common in fault-tolerant quantum computing, such as measurement-dependent Pauli corrections.
AI.method: Generalizes polynomial-time outcome-complete simulation algorithm to track global phases exactly, creating phased outcome-complete simulation. This enables equivalence checking for stabilizer circuits augmented with single-qubit rotations exp(iαZ) by symbolic angles, handling all measurement outcomes and input states simultaneously.
AI.result: Developed efficient classical verification method that can check equivalence of circuits containing symbolic-angle rotations, outcome-parity-conditional Pauli gates, and intermediate measurements. The method works for all values of symbolic angles and all measurement outcomes, given proper angle correspondence and outcome mapping.
AI.conclusion: The phased outcome-complete simulation algorithm provides practical verification tools for compilation algorithms in fault-tolerant quantum computing, enabling testing of transformations that preserve rotation angles while modifying Clifford portions of circuits.

title: Coefficient-Decoupled Matrix Product Operators as an Interface to Linear-Combination-of-Unitaries Circuits
summary: We introduce a coefficient-decoupled matrix product operator (MPO) representation for Pauli-sum operators that separates reusable symbolic operator support from a tunable coefficient bridge across a fixed bipartition. This representation provides a direct interface to linear-combination-of-unitaries (LCU) circuits: the symbolic left/right dictionaries define a static \textsc{Select} oracle that is compiled once, while coefficient updates modify only a dynamic \textsc{Prep} oracle. As a proof of concept, we construct compact state-adapted Pauli pools by sampling Pauli strings from a pretrained matrix product state (MPS), pruning them to a fixed symbolic pool, optimizing only their coefficients, and transferring the resulting weights directly to the LCU interface. The resulting workflow provides a reusable classical-to-quantum compilation strategy in which the symbolic operator structure is compiled once, and subsequent updates are confined to a low-dimensional coefficient object.

AI.tldr: A coefficient-decoupled MPO representation for Pauli-sum operators that separates symbolic structure from tunable coefficients, enabling reusable quantum compilation with static Select oracles and dynamic Prep oracles.
AI.motivation: To create a more efficient quantum compilation workflow for Pauli-sum operators by decoupling reusable symbolic operator structure from tunable coefficients, enabling one-time compilation of static components and reducing subsequent updates to low-dimensional coefficient optimization.
AI.method: Introduces a coefficient-decoupled MPO representation that separates symbolic operator support from coefficient bridges across bipartitions. Uses this representation as direct interface to LCU circuits with static Select oracles (compiled once) and dynamic Prep oracles. Constructs compact state-adapted Pauli pools by sampling from pretrained MPS, pruning to fixed symbolic pool, optimizing coefficients, and transferring weights to LCU interface.
AI.result: Provides a reusable classical-to-quantum compilation strategy where symbolic operator structure is compiled once, and subsequent updates are confined to low-dimensional coefficient objects, enabling efficient coefficient optimization without recompiling quantum circuits.
AI.conclusion: The coefficient-decoupled MPO representation enables efficient quantum compilation workflows with separation of concerns between static symbolic structure and dynamic coefficients, facilitating reusable quantum circuit components and streamlined optimization processes.

title: Quantum Spectral Authentication under Public Unitary Challenges
summary: We introduce Quantum Spectral Authentication (QSA), a primitive for verifying that a remote quantum endpoint still possesses a previously installed secret quantum resource, such as a hidden state or state-preparation capability, without revealing that secret. QSA uses fresh public unitary challenges and spectral features of the planted state to derive transcript-bound session material for explicit authentication. We analyse attack strategies including eigenstate propagation across challenges, repeated-session leakage, and direct online forgery. For practical implementation, we develop a symmetric verifier-driven unitary compiler compatible with low-depth quantum phase estimation. Simulations indicate that this symmetric fast-power construction is substantially more noise tolerant than an asymmetric alternative, and small-instance experiments on IBM ibm_fez provide a hardware sanity check. QSA therefore offers a plausible near-term authentication layer for quantum networks and control-plane applications.

AI.tldr: Quantum Spectral Authentication (QSA) enables remote verification of secret quantum resources without revealing them, using public unitary challenges and spectral analysis for authentication.
AI.motivation: To create a practical authentication layer for quantum networks and control-plane applications that can verify possession of secret quantum resources (like hidden states or state-preparation capabilities) without exposing those secrets, addressing the need for quantum endpoint authentication in near-term quantum systems.
AI.method: Uses fresh public unitary challenges and spectral features of the planted state to derive transcript-bound session material for explicit authentication. Includes a symmetric verifier-driven unitary compiler compatible with low-depth quantum phase estimation, with a symmetric fast-power construction for noise tolerance.
AI.result: Simulations show the symmetric fast-power construction is substantially more noise tolerant than asymmetric alternatives. Small-instance experiments on IBM ibm_fez hardware provide validation. The method resists attacks including eigenstate propagation across challenges, repeated-session leakage, and direct online forgery.
AI.conclusion: QSA offers a plausible near-term authentication layer for quantum networks and control-plane applications, providing a way to verify quantum endpoint possession of secret resources without revealing those secrets.

title: The Pareto Frontiers of Magic and Entanglement: The Case of Two Qubits
summary: Magic and entanglement are two measures that are widely used to characterize quantum resources. We study the interplay between magic and entanglement in two-qubit systems, focusing on the two extremes: maximal magic and minimal magic for a given level of entanglement. We quantify magic by the Rényi entropy of order 2, $M_2$, and entanglement by the concurrence $Δ$. We find that the Pareto frontier of maximal magic $M_2^{(max)}(Δ)$ is composed of three separate segments, while the boundary of minimal magic $M_2^{(min)}(Δ)$ is a single continuous line. We derive simple analytical formulas for all these four cases, and explicitly parametrize all distinct quantum states of maximal or minimal magic at a given level of entanglement.

AI.tldr: Analysis of magic-entanglement trade-off in two-qubit systems, identifying Pareto frontiers for maximal and minimal magic at given entanglement levels.
AI.motivation: To understand the interplay between two key quantum resource measures - magic and entanglement - in two-qubit systems, specifically investigating the extremes of maximal and minimal magic for fixed entanglement levels.
AI.method: Quantify magic using Rényi entropy of order 2 (M₂) and entanglement using concurrence (Δ). Analyze Pareto frontiers for maximal magic M₂^(max)(Δ) and minimal magic M₂^(min)(Δ) in two-qubit systems.
AI.result: The maximal magic frontier consists of three separate segments, while the minimal magic boundary is a single continuous line. Analytical formulas derived for all four cases, with explicit parametrization of quantum states achieving these extremes.
AI.conclusion: The study reveals distinct structural patterns in the magic-entanglement trade-off for two-qubit systems, providing complete analytical characterization of extreme states and their boundaries.

title: Test of the essential collapse-locality loophole
comment: Main text with 5 pages, 3 figures, 1 table; Supplementary Information with 5 pages and 4 figures
summary: Collapse-locality is an untested loophole in the violation of Bell's inequalities. The core of the argument is that the time value of photon detection is delayed by the time Tc required by the collapse of its quantum state. The value of Tc is given by the underlying theory of quantum collapse, and is mostly unknown. Depending on the value of Tc, detections in the performed Bell's experiments may have not been truly space-like separated events. This implies that the inequalities may have been violated as a consequence of (conspiratorial) information propagating at subluminal speed. We report an optical Bell experiment which closes the weaker ('essential') form of this loophole regardless the theory of quantum collapse. This is possible thanks to unique features of the setup. These features are: classical signals sent to the stations to define a time reference, and variable distance between the stations leaving all other parameters constant.

AI.tldr: Optical Bell experiment closes the collapse-locality loophole by ensuring space-like separation regardless of quantum collapse theory, using classical time references and variable station distances.
AI.motivation: Address the collapse-locality loophole in Bell inequality violations, where photon detection timing could be delayed by quantum state collapse time (Tc), potentially allowing subluminal information transfer and invalidating space-like separation claims in previous experiments.
AI.method: Optical Bell experiment with two key features: (1) classical signals sent to stations to establish precise time reference, and (2) variable distance between measurement stations while keeping all other experimental parameters constant, enabling verification of space-like separation independent of quantum collapse theory.
AI.result: The experiment successfully closes the weaker 'essential' form of the collapse-locality loophole, demonstrating that Bell inequality violations cannot be explained by conspiratorial subluminal information transfer regardless of the unknown collapse time Tc in any quantum collapse theory.
AI.conclusion: The collapse-locality loophole can be experimentally closed using classical timing references and variable station distances, strengthening the evidence for quantum nonlocality and the violation of local realism in Bell tests.

title: Measurement-induced non-commutativity in adaptive fermionic linear optics
summary: Fermionic linear optics (FLO) with Gaussian resources is efficiently classically simulable. We show that this is no longer the case for such quantum circuits for fermions with internal degrees of freedom, equipped with mid-circuit number monitoring and classical feedforward. In our architecture, the measurement record routes the selected blocks into a fixed-order Bell-fusion pairing geometry. On the level of classical description, this implies realizing a situation in which the permutation sum no longer collapses to a single determinant or Pfaffian. Each post-selected branch expands as a signed sum of path-ordered products of typically non-commuting dressed blocks, and branch amplitudes are matrix elements of the resulting non-commutative trace polynomials. Numerically, we observe Porter-Thomas statistics as the output distribution and a rapid growth of the minimal order-respecting matrix product operator bond dimension. These results thus establish mid-circuit measurement-induced non-commutativity as a route to sampling hardness for noninteracting fermions under reasonable complexity assumptions, without introducing coherent two-body interactions into the FLO evolution.

AI.tldr: Fermionic linear optics with Gaussian resources is classically simulable, but adding internal degrees of freedom, mid-circuit measurements, and classical feedforward creates sampling hardness without introducing two-body interactions.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate that fermionic linear optics (FLO) circuits, which are classically simulable with Gaussian resources, can become computationally hard when enhanced with internal degrees of freedom, mid-circuit measurements, and classical feedforward, without requiring coherent two-body interactions.
AI.method: Extend FLO circuits with fermions having internal degrees of freedom, incorporate mid-circuit number monitoring and classical feedforward, use measurement records to route selected blocks into fixed-order Bell-fusion pairing geometry, analyze classical description through permutation sums that no longer collapse to single determinants/Pfaffians, and study post-selected branches as signed sums of path-ordered products of non-commuting dressed blocks.
AI.result: Numerical observations show Porter-Thomas statistics in output distributions and rapid growth of minimal order-respecting matrix product operator bond dimension, establishing sampling hardness for noninteracting fermions under reasonable complexity assumptions.
AI.conclusion: Mid-circuit measurement-induced non-commutativity provides a route to sampling hardness for noninteracting fermions without introducing coherent two-body interactions into FLO evolution, demonstrating that FLO circuits can become computationally hard with appropriate enhancements.

title: Uncertainty Quantification for Quantum Computing
summary: This review is designed to introduce mathematicians and computational scientists to quantum computing (QC) through the lens of uncertainty quantification (UQ) by presenting a mathematically rigorous and accessible narrative for understanding how noise and intrinsic randomness shape quantum computational outcomes in the language of mathematics. By grounding quantum computation in statistical inference, we highlight how mathematical tools such as probabilistic modeling, stochastic analysis, Bayesian inference, and sensitivity analysis, can directly address error propagation and reliability challenges in today's quantum devices. We also connect these methods to key scientific priorities in the field, including scalable uncertainty-aware algorithms and characterization of correlated errors. The purpose is to narrow the conceptual divide between applied mathematics, scientific computing and quantum information sciences, demonstrating how mathematically rooted UQ methodologies can guide validation, error mitigation, and principled algorithm design for emerging quantum technologies, in order to address challenges and opportunities present in modern-day quantum high performance and fault-tolerant quantum computing paradigms.

AI.tldr: A review introducing mathematicians and computational scientists to quantum computing through uncertainty quantification, showing how mathematical tools can address noise and reliability challenges in quantum devices.
AI.motivation: To bridge the conceptual gap between applied mathematics/scientific computing and quantum information sciences by demonstrating how mathematically rigorous uncertainty quantification can address fundamental challenges in quantum computing related to noise, error propagation, and reliability.
AI.method: Presents quantum computing through the lens of uncertainty quantification, grounding quantum computation in statistical inference and applying mathematical tools including probabilistic modeling, stochastic analysis, Bayesian inference, and sensitivity analysis to address error propagation and reliability challenges.
AI.result: The review connects mathematical UQ methodologies to key scientific priorities in quantum computing, including scalable uncertainty-aware algorithms and characterization of correlated errors, demonstrating how these approaches can guide validation, error mitigation, and principled algorithm design.
AI.conclusion: Mathematically rooted uncertainty quantification methodologies provide essential tools for addressing challenges in modern quantum computing paradigms, including high-performance and fault-tolerant quantum computing, by enabling systematic approaches to validation, error mitigation, and algorithm design.

title: Neural Operator Quantum State: A Foundation Model for Quantum Dynamics
summary: Capturing the dynamics of quantum many-body systems under time-dependent driving protocols is a central challenge for numerical simulations. Existing methods such as tensor networks and time-dependent neural quantum states, however, must be re-run for every protocol. In this work, we introduce the Neural Operator Quantum State (NOQS) as a foundation model for quantum dynamics. Rather than solving the Schrödinger equation for individual trajectories, our approach aims to \emph{learn the solution operator} that maps entire driving protocols to time-evolved quantum states. Once trained, the NOQS predicts time evolution under unseen protocols in a single forward pass, requiring no additional optimization. We validate NOQS on the two-dimensional Ising model with time-dependent longitudinal and transverse fields, demonstrating accurate prediction not only for unseen in-distribution protocols, but also for qualitatively different, out-of-distribution functional forms of driving. Further, a single NOQS model can be transferred between different temporal resolutions, and can be efficiently fine-tuned with sparse experimental measurements to improve predictions across all observables at negligible cost. Our work introduces a new paradigm for quantum dynamics simulation and provides a practical computational-experimental interface for driven quantum systems.

AI.tldr: NOQS is a foundation model that learns the solution operator mapping driving protocols to time-evolved quantum states, enabling single-pass predictions for unseen protocols without re-optimization.
AI.motivation: Existing quantum dynamics simulation methods (tensor networks, time-dependent neural quantum states) require re-running for every driving protocol, lacking efficiency for exploring parameter spaces or experimental interfaces.
AI.method: Neural Operator Quantum State (NOQS) learns the solution operator that maps entire driving protocols to time-evolved quantum states, trained on protocol-state pairs, enabling single forward-pass predictions for unseen protocols.
AI.result: NOQS accurately predicts dynamics for 2D Ising model with time-dependent fields, including unseen in-distribution protocols and out-of-distribution functional forms; supports temporal resolution transfer and efficient fine-tuning with sparse measurements.
AI.conclusion: NOQS introduces a new paradigm for quantum dynamics simulation as a foundation model, providing a practical computational-experimental interface for driven quantum systems with efficient protocol exploration.

title: T Count as a Numerically Solvable Minimization Problem
summary: We present a formulation of the problem of finding the smallest T -Count circuit that implements a given unitary as a binary search over a sequence of continuous minimization problems, and demonstrate that these problems are numerically solvable in practice. We reproduce best-known results for synthesis of circuits with a small number of qubits, and push the bounds of the largest circuits that can be solved for in this way. Additionally, we show that circuit partitioning can be used to adapt this technique to be used to optimize the T -Count of circuits with large numbers of qubits by breaking the circuit into a series of smaller sub-circuits that can be optimized independently.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a method for finding minimal T-count quantum circuits using binary search over continuous optimization problems, showing practical numerical solvability and extending to larger circuits via partitioning.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to develop practical methods for synthesizing quantum circuits with minimal T-count (a key resource in fault-tolerant quantum computing) for larger circuits than previously possible, addressing the computational complexity of exact T-count minimization.
AI.method: The method formulates T-count minimization as binary search over a sequence of continuous minimization problems, which are numerically solvable in practice. Additionally, circuit partitioning is used to handle large circuits by breaking them into smaller sub-circuits that can be optimized independently.
AI.result: The approach reproduces best-known results for small-qubit circuits and pushes the bounds of solvable circuit sizes. It demonstrates that circuit partitioning enables T-count optimization for circuits with large numbers of qubits that were previously intractable.
AI.conclusion: The continuous optimization approach provides a practical method for T-count minimization that scales to larger circuits through partitioning, offering a viable path for optimizing fault-tolerant quantum circuits beyond current limitations.

title: Optimal measurement-based quantum thermal machines in a finite-size system
summary: We present a measurement-based quantum thermal machine that extracts work from the back-action of generalized quantum measurements whose working medium is a coupled two-level quantum system. Specifically, we derive universal optimization criteria for a three-stroke measurement-based engine cycle with coupled two-level system of Ising-like interaction as a working medium. Furthermore, we present two numerical algorithms to optimize the engine work extraction and enhance its performance. Our numerical results demonstrate: (i) efficiency peaks in the projective-measurement limit; (ii) symmetry breaking (detuning or weak coupling) enlarges the exploitable energy gap; and (iii) performance remains robust ($>50\%$ of optimum) under $\sim\!10^\circ$ feedback-pulse errors. The framework is platform-agnostic and directly implementable with current superconducting, trapped-ion, or NMR technologies, providing a concrete route to scalable, measurement-powered quantum thermal machines.

AI.tldr: Measurement-based quantum thermal machine using coupled two-level system extracts work from quantum measurement back-action, with optimization algorithms showing efficiency peaks in projective limit and robustness to errors.
AI.motivation: To develop a practical, scalable quantum thermal machine that harnesses quantum measurement back-action for work extraction, leveraging current quantum technologies like superconducting qubits, trapped ions, or NMR systems.
AI.method: Three-stroke measurement-based engine cycle using coupled two-level quantum system with Ising-like interaction as working medium; derivation of universal optimization criteria; development of two numerical algorithms for optimizing work extraction and enhancing performance.
AI.result: Efficiency peaks in projective-measurement limit; symmetry breaking (detuning or weak coupling) enlarges exploitable energy gap; performance remains robust (>50% of optimum) under ~10° feedback-pulse errors; framework is platform-agnostic and directly implementable with current quantum technologies.
AI.conclusion: The measurement-based quantum thermal machine provides a concrete, scalable route to harnessing quantum measurement back-action for work extraction, with robust performance characteristics that make it suitable for implementation across various current quantum technology platforms.

title: Reinforcement learning for quantum processes with memory
summary: In reinforcement learning, an agent interacts sequentially with an environment to maximize a reward, receiving only partial, probabilistic feedback. This creates a fundamental exploration-exploitation trade-off: the agent must explore to learn the hidden dynamics while exploiting this knowledge to maximize its target objective. While extensively studied classically, applying this framework to quantum systems requires dealing with hidden quantum states that evolve via unknown dynamics. We formalize this problem via a framework where the environment maintains a hidden quantum memory evolving via unknown quantum channels, and the agent intervenes sequentially using quantum instruments. For this setting, we adapt an optimistic maximum-likelihood estimation algorithm. We extend the analysis to continuous action spaces, allowing us to model general positive operator-valued measures (POVMs). By controlling the propagation of estimation errors through quantum channels and instruments, we prove that the cumulative regret of our strategy scales as $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{K})$ over $K$ episodes. Furthermore, via a reduction to the multi-armed quantum bandit problem, we establish information-theoretic lower bounds demonstrating that this sublinear scaling is strictly optimal up to polylogarithmic factors. As a physical application, we consider state-agnostic work extraction. When extracting free energy from a sequence of non-i.i.d. quantum states correlated by a hidden memory, any lack of knowledge about the source leads to thermodynamic dissipation. In our setting, the mathematical regret exactly quantifies this cumulative dissipation. Using our adaptive algorithm, the agent uses past energy outcomes to improve its extraction protocol on the fly, achieving sublinear cumulative dissipation, and, consequently, an asymptotically zero dissipation rate.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a quantum reinforcement learning framework for environments with hidden quantum memory, develops an optimistic maximum-likelihood algorithm with $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{K})$ regret, proves optimality via information-theoretic lower bounds, and applies it to state-agnostic work extraction achieving asymptotically zero dissipation rate.
AI.motivation: Classical reinforcement learning's exploration-exploitation trade-off needs adaptation to quantum systems where environments maintain hidden quantum states evolving via unknown quantum channels. There's a need for quantum RL algorithms that can handle continuous action spaces (general POVMs) and provide theoretical guarantees for quantum environments with memory.
AI.method: Formalizes quantum RL framework where environment maintains hidden quantum memory evolving via unknown quantum channels, agent intervenes sequentially using quantum instruments. Adapts optimistic maximum-likelihood estimation algorithm, extends analysis to continuous action spaces to model general POVMs. Controls propagation of estimation errors through quantum channels and instruments.
AI.result: Proves cumulative regret scales as $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{K})$ over K episodes. Establishes information-theoretic lower bounds showing this sublinear scaling is strictly optimal up to polylogarithmic factors via reduction to multi-armed quantum bandit problem. For state-agnostic work extraction, achieves sublinear cumulative dissipation and asymptotically zero dissipation rate.
AI.conclusion: The framework successfully adapts classical RL concepts to quantum settings with hidden memory, providing theoretically optimal algorithms with practical applications in quantum thermodynamics. The regret-dissipation equivalence enables adaptive work extraction protocols that learn from past outcomes to minimize thermodynamic dissipation in non-i.i.d. quantum systems.

title: Banach and counting measures, and dynamics of singular quantum states generated by averaging of operator random walks
summary:
In this paper the random channels and their compositions in the space of quantum states are studied.
  For compositions of i.i.d. random unitary channels, the limit behaviour of probability distributions is described.
  The sufficient condition for convergence in probability is obtained.
  The generalized convergence in distribution w.r.t. weak operator topology is obtained.
  The analysis of transmission of pure and normal states to the set of singular states is done. The dynamics of quantum states is described in terms of the evolution of the values of quadratic forms of operators from the algebra that implements the representation of canonical commutation relations.

AI.tldr: Analysis of random quantum channels and their compositions, focusing on convergence properties and state transmission dynamics in quantum systems.
AI.motivation: To understand the statistical behavior of random quantum channels and their compositions, particularly their convergence properties and how they transform different types of quantum states, which is crucial for quantum information theory and quantum dynamics.
AI.method: Study compositions of i.i.d. random unitary channels, analyze probability distributions, establish convergence conditions in probability and distribution (weak operator topology), and examine transmission of pure/normal states to singular states using quadratic forms from CCR algebra representations.
AI.result: Obtained sufficient condition for convergence in probability, established generalized convergence in distribution w.r.t. weak operator topology, and analyzed state transmission dynamics between pure, normal, and singular quantum states.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides mathematical foundations for understanding random quantum channel compositions, their convergence properties, and state transformation dynamics, contributing to quantum information theory and statistical quantum mechanics.

title: Chiral quantum batteries
summary: Exploiting quantum effects for energy storage, quantum batteries (QBs) offer compelling advantages over conventional ones in terms of superior energy density, ultrafast charging, and high conversion efficiency. However, their realization is hampered by decoherence, which causes incomplete charging, rapid self-discharging, and reduced extractable work. Here, we propose a QB architecture based on a chiral magnonic platform. It comprises two yttrium iron garnet (YIG) spheres, one serving as the charger and the other as the QB, coupled to a waveguide. The unique chiral coupling between magnons and the guided electromagnetic fields breaks inversion symmetry, inducing both nonreciprocal energy flow and coherent interference between the charger and QB. Their synergy endows our QB with a 34-fold increase in energy capacity and a 55-fold boost in extractable work compared to its achiral counterpart in an experimentally accessible regime. Our scheme harnesses the decoherence from the electromagnetic fields and turns its destruction into an asset, which enables the robustness and wireless-like remote charging features of the QB. Our analysis reveals that these extraordinary capabilities stem from quantum coherence. By establishing chirality as a useful quantum resource, our work paves a viable path toward the realization of QBs.

AI.tldr: Chiral magnonic quantum battery achieves 34x higher energy capacity and 55x more extractable work than achiral counterparts by exploiting quantum coherence and nonreciprocal energy flow.
AI.motivation: Quantum batteries offer superior energy density and charging speed but face decoherence issues that cause incomplete charging, self-discharging, and reduced extractable work. Current implementations struggle with these quantum decoherence challenges.
AI.method: Proposes a chiral magnonic QB architecture using two yttrium iron garnet (YIG) spheres (charger and battery) coupled to a waveguide. Exploits chiral coupling between magnons and guided electromagnetic fields to break inversion symmetry, creating nonreciprocal energy flow and coherent interference between charger and QB.
AI.result: Achieves 34-fold increase in energy capacity and 55-fold boost in extractable work compared to achiral counterpart in experimentally accessible regime. Demonstrates robustness and wireless-like remote charging by harnessing decoherence from electromagnetic fields.
AI.conclusion: Chirality serves as a valuable quantum resource for quantum batteries, enabling superior performance by exploiting quantum coherence. This work establishes a viable path toward practical QB realization by turning decoherence from a liability into an asset.

title: The 27-qubit Counterexample to the LU-LC Conjecture is Minimal
summary: It was once conjectured that two graph states are local unitary (LU) equivalent if and only if they are local Clifford (LC) equivalent. This so-called LU-LC conjecture was disproved in 2007, as a pair of 27-qubit graph states that are LU-equivalent, but not LC-equivalent, was discovered. We prove that this counterexample to the LU-LC conjecture is minimal. In other words, for graph states on up to 26 qubits, the notions of LU-equivalence and LC-equivalence coincide. This result is obtained by studying the structure of 2-local complementation, a special case of the recently introduced r-local complementation, and a generalization of the well-known local complementation. We make use of a connection with triorthogonal codes and Reed-Muller codes.

AI.tldr: The paper proves that the minimal counterexample to the LU-LC conjecture is 27 qubits, showing that for graph states up to 26 qubits, LU-equivalence and LC-equivalence coincide.
AI.motivation: The LU-LC conjecture (that local unitary equivalence implies local Clifford equivalence for graph states) was disproved in 2007 with a 27-qubit counterexample. The motivation is to determine whether this counterexample is minimal and to understand the boundary where the conjecture fails.
AI.method: The authors study the structure of 2-local complementation (a special case of r-local complementation and generalization of local complementation), and establish connections with triorthogonal codes and Reed-Muller codes to analyze graph state equivalences.
AI.result: The paper proves that the 27-qubit counterexample is indeed minimal: for all graph states on up to 26 qubits, LU-equivalence implies LC-equivalence. The boundary where the conjecture fails is precisely at 27 qubits.
AI.conclusion: The LU-LC conjecture holds for graph states with up to 26 qubits, and the known 27-qubit counterexample is minimal. This establishes the precise threshold where the equivalence between LU and LC operations breaks down for graph states.

title: Epitaxial CeO2 Films as a Host for Quantum Applications
summary: In highly purified host, the coherence of quantum emitters is ultimately limited by hyperfine interactions between the emitter and lattice nuclei possessing non-zero nuclear magnetic moments. This limitation can only be mitigated through isotopic purification. In this work, we investigate CeO2 as a host composed entirely of nuclei with zero nuclear moment. High-quality CeO2 thin films were grown by PLD and doped with Tm and Er ions. Structural characterization using X-ray diffraction, atomic force microscopy, and ion channeling confirms single-crystalline, atomically smooth films with dopants substitutionally incorporated at Ce lattice sites. Photoluminescence lifetime measurements show significantly longer lifetimes for Er-doped CeO2 (2.9 - 5.3 ms) compared with Tm-doped films (14 - 68 μs). Moreover, the Er-doped PLD films exhibit longer lifetimes at ~1% dopant concentration than previously reported for MBE-grown films. Density functional theory calculations reveal a substantial overlap between unoccupied O 2p and Tm 4f states near the valence band maximum, whereas Er 4f states remain well isolated. This electronic interaction likely introduces non-radiative recombination pathways in Tm-doped CeO2, explaining the reduced lifetimes. These findings highlight the importance of selecting appropriate dopant-host combinations and optimized growth conditions to minimize non-radiative channels for quantum applications.

AI.tldr: CeO2 as a zero-nuclear-moment host for quantum emitters shows longer photoluminescence lifetimes for Er doping than Tm doping due to electronic interactions enabling non-radiative recombination in Tm-doped films.
AI.motivation: To overcome hyperfine interaction limitations in quantum emitters by investigating CeO2 as a host composed entirely of nuclei with zero nuclear magnetic moments, enabling isotopic purification-free coherence enhancement.
AI.method: Grew high-quality CeO2 thin films by pulsed laser deposition (PLD), doped with Tm and Er ions. Used XRD, AFM, and ion channeling for structural characterization. Measured photoluminescence lifetimes and performed density functional theory calculations to analyze electronic interactions.
AI.result: Er-doped CeO2 showed significantly longer lifetimes (2.9-5.3 ms) compared to Tm-doped films (14-68 μs). DFT revealed substantial overlap between unoccupied O 2p and Tm 4f states near valence band maximum, while Er 4f states remained isolated, explaining the lifetime differences.
AI.conclusion: CeO2 is a promising zero-nuclear-moment host for quantum applications, but dopant selection is critical. Er is superior to Tm due to isolated 4f states that minimize non-radiative recombination pathways, highlighting the importance of optimized dopant-host combinations and growth conditions.

title: Superconducting Parallel-Plate Resonators for the Detection of Single Electron Spins
comment: 12 pages, 7 figures, plus supplementary material of 5 pages, 4 figures
summary: We introduce a multilayer superconducting microwave resonator with sub-Ohm impedance optimized for high coupling strength to single electron spins. The design minimizes the magnetic far-field and therefore achieves a Purcell factor $F_P > 10^{15}$. We show several ways to fabricate this type of resonator and present resonators with an intrinsic $Q$-factor exceeding $2 \cdot 10^4$ at the single-photon level. We further characterize these resonators in magnetic fields up to $500 \, \text{mT}$. Finally, we evaluate the impact of the achievable Purcell factor on single-spin detection through photon counting and dispersive readout.

AI.tldr: Multilayer superconducting microwave resonator with sub-Ohm impedance achieves Purcell factor >10¹⁵ for strong coupling to single electron spins, with Q-factor >2×10⁴ and operation in magnetic fields up to 500 mT.
AI.motivation: To achieve high coupling strength between microwave resonators and single electron spins for quantum information processing applications, requiring strong Purcell enhancement for efficient spin-photon interaction.
AI.method: Developed multilayer superconducting microwave resonator design with sub-Ohm impedance that minimizes magnetic far-field. Explored several fabrication approaches and characterized resonators at single-photon level and in magnetic fields up to 500 mT.
AI.result: Achieved Purcell factor FP > 10¹⁵, intrinsic Q-factor exceeding 2×10⁴ at single-photon level, and successful operation in magnetic fields up to 500 mT. Demonstrated impact on single-spin detection through photon counting and dispersive readout.
AI.conclusion: The developed multilayer superconducting resonator design enables unprecedented Purcell enhancement for coupling to single electron spins, providing a promising platform for quantum information processing with spins and microwave photons.

title: Causality is rare: some topological properties of causal quantum channels
summary: Sorkin's impossible operations demonstrate that causality of a quantum channel in QFT is an additional constraint on quantum operations above and beyond the locality of the channel. What has not been shown in the literature so far is how much of a constraint it is. Here we answer this question in perhaps the strongest possible terms: the set of causal channels is nowhere dense in the set of local channels. We connect this result to quantum information, showing that the set of causal unitaries has Haar measure $0$ in the set of all unitaries acting on a lattice. Finally, we close with discussion on the implications and connections to recent QFT measurement models.

AI.tldr: Causal quantum channels in QFT are nowhere dense in local channels, and causal unitaries have Haar measure zero among all lattice unitaries.
AI.motivation: Sorkin's impossible operations show causality is an additional constraint beyond locality for quantum channels in QFT, but the extent of this constraint hasn't been quantified. The paper aims to determine how restrictive causality is compared to locality.
AI.method: Mathematical analysis of the topological structure of causal vs. local channels in QFT, connecting to measure theory in quantum information by examining Haar measure of causal unitaries on lattices.
AI.result: The set of causal channels is nowhere dense in the set of local channels, meaning causal channels form an extremely sparse subset. Additionally, causal unitaries have Haar measure zero in the set of all unitaries acting on a lattice.
AI.conclusion: Causality imposes a much stronger constraint than locality alone, making causal operations exceptionally rare among local operations. This has implications for QFT measurement models and suggests causality is a highly restrictive principle in quantum field theory.

title: Engineering energy-time entanglement from resonance fluorescence
comment: 35 pages, 5 figures; incl. Supplementary Information (SI) with 7 SI figures, 1 SI tables;
summary: Resonance fluorescence from a coherently driven two-level emitter is a minimal quantum optical field that combines phase coherence with single-photon-level nonlinearity. Here we show that it can be engineered, using only passive linear interferometry, into energy-time entanglement. By injecting resonance fluorescence from a single quantum dot into an asymmetric Mach--Zehnder interferometer operated near destructive interference of the single-photon component, we generate an output field whose coincidence statistics are dominated by the simultaneous two-photon contribution |2> and the temporally separated photon-pair contribution |11>. In a Franson geometry, these two sectors are resolved on the coincidence-delay axis, and both exhibit high-visibility nonlocal interference fringes and violate the Clauser--Horne--Shimony--Holt Bell inequality. Our results reveal a general route for engineering entanglement from resonance fluorescence using passive optics.

AI.tldr: Resonance fluorescence from a quantum dot can be engineered into energy-time entanglement using passive linear interferometry, generating nonlocal interference and Bell inequality violation.
AI.motivation: Resonance fluorescence from coherently driven two-level emitters combines phase coherence with single-photon nonlinearity, making it a promising source for quantum optics applications, but its potential for generating entanglement through passive methods remains unexplored.
AI.method: Inject resonance fluorescence from a single quantum dot into an asymmetric Mach-Zehnder interferometer operated near destructive interference of single-photon components, generating output dominated by simultaneous two-photon (|2>) and temporally separated photon-pair (|11>) contributions, then analyze in a Franson geometry.
AI.result: The engineered field exhibits high-visibility nonlocal interference fringes in both |2> and |11> sectors, with both violating the Clauser-Horne-Shimony-Holt Bell inequality, demonstrating genuine energy-time entanglement.
AI.conclusion: Passive linear interferometry provides a general route for engineering entanglement from resonance fluorescence, enabling quantum information applications without active components.

title: Can every set of incompatible measurements lead to genuine multipartite steering?
summary: Measurement incompatibility and bipartite quantum steering are known to display a strong connection: a set of measurements is incompatible if and only if it can lead to bipartite steering. Despite such a close link between these concepts in bipartite scenarios, little is known in the multipartite setting, where notions of genuine multipartite correlations play major roles. In this work we prove that, as in the bipartite case, incompatibility is also necessary and sufficient for genuine multipartite steering in any multipartite scenario with a single uncharacterised party. Interestingly, genuine multipartite steering can be extracted from any set of incompatible measurements using states which are not SLOCC equivalent, such as GHZ and W states. In contrast, we prove that this result does not hold in scenarios with more than one uncharacterised party, by presenting a set of incompatible measurements that can never lead to genuine multipartite steering in these cases. In order to obtain our main results, we introduce methods tailored for multipartite correlations, paving the way to understanding the role of measurement incompatibility beyond bipartite scenarios.

AI.tldr: Measurement incompatibility is necessary and sufficient for genuine multipartite steering with a single uncharacterized party, but not with multiple uncharacterized parties.
AI.motivation: While measurement incompatibility and bipartite quantum steering are known to be equivalent, little is known about their relationship in multipartite scenarios where genuine multipartite correlations play crucial roles.
AI.method: The authors prove theoretical results about the relationship between measurement incompatibility and genuine multipartite steering. They introduce methods tailored for multipartite correlations and analyze scenarios with different numbers of uncharacterized parties.
AI.result: 1) Incompatibility is necessary and sufficient for genuine multipartite steering in any multipartite scenario with a single uncharacterized party. 2) Genuine multipartite steering can be extracted from any set of incompatible measurements using states not SLOCC equivalent (e.g., GHZ and W states). 3) This equivalence breaks down with more than one uncharacterized party, as demonstrated by presenting incompatible measurements that never lead to genuine multipartite steering.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes fundamental connections between measurement incompatibility and genuine multipartite steering, showing the equivalence holds for single uncharacterized parties but not for multiple uncharacterized parties, providing new insights into multipartite quantum correlations.

title: Weak distillation of quantum resources
summary: Importance sampling based on quasi-probability decomposition is the backbone of many widely used techniques, such as error mitigation, circuit knitting, and, more generally, virtual quantum resource distillation, as it allows one to simulate operations that are not accessible in a given setting. However, this class of protocols faces a fundamental problem -- it only allows to estimate expectation values. Here, we provide a general framework that lifts any quasi-probability-based protocol from expectation value estimation to a weak simulator, realizing sampling from the desired distribution only using a restricted class of quantum resources. Our method runs with the sampling cost proportional to the negativity of the quasi-probability, in stark contrast to the naive estimation-based approach that requires a large number of samples even in the case of small negativity. We show that our method requires significantly fewer samples in a number of relevant scenarios, such as error mitigation, entanglement distillation and magic state distillation. Our framework realizes the weak simulation of quantum resources without actually distilling the state, introducing a new notion of quantum resource distillation.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a framework that transforms quasi-probability-based protocols from expectation value estimation to weak simulation, enabling sampling from desired distributions using restricted quantum resources with sampling cost proportional to quasi-probability negativity.
AI.motivation: Quasi-probability decomposition methods (used in error mitigation, circuit knitting, virtual resource distillation) are fundamentally limited to expectation value estimation, not sampling from distributions. The authors aim to overcome this limitation by developing a framework that enables weak simulation (sampling) rather than just expectation value estimation.
AI.method: The authors develop a general framework that lifts any quasi-probability-based protocol to a weak simulator. The method enables sampling from desired distributions using only restricted quantum resources, with sampling cost scaling proportionally to the negativity of the quasi-probability decomposition, in contrast to naive estimation-based approaches.
AI.result: The framework demonstrates significantly reduced sample requirements compared to naive approaches in multiple scenarios: error mitigation, entanglement distillation, and magic state distillation. It achieves weak simulation of quantum resources without physically distilling the states, introducing a new notion of quantum resource distillation.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a fundamental advancement in quasi-probability methods by enabling weak simulation (sampling) rather than just expectation value estimation, with practical advantages in sample efficiency across various quantum computing applications including error mitigation and resource distillation.

title: Optimizing Entanglement Distribution Protocols: Maximizing Classical Information in Quantum Networks
summary: Efficient entanglement distribution is the foundational challenge in realizing large-scale Quantum Networks. However, state-of-the-art solutions are frequently limited by restrictive operational assumptions, prohibitive computational complexities, and performance metrics that misalign with practical application needs. To overcome these barriers, this paper addresses the entanglement distribution problem by introducing four pivotal advances. First, recognizing that the primary application of quantum communication is the transmission of private information, we derive the Ensemble Capacity (EC), a novel metric that explicitly quantifies the secure classical information enabled by the entanglement distribution. Second, we propose a generalized mathematical formulation that removes legacy structural restrictions in the solution space. Our formulation supports an unconstrained, arbitrary sequencing of entanglement swapping and purification. Third, to efficiently navigate the resulting combinatorial optimization space, we introduce a novel Dynamic Programming (DP)-based hypergraph generation algorithm. Unlike prior methods, our approach avoids artificial fidelity quantization, preserving exact, continuous fidelities while proactively pruning sub-optimal trajectories. Finally, we encapsulate these algorithmic solutions into CODE, a system-level, two-tiered orchestration framework designed to enable near-real-time network responsiveness. Extensive evaluations confirm that our DP-driven architecture yields superior private classical information capacity and significant reductions in computational complexity, successfully meeting the strict sub-second latency thresholds required for dynamic QN operation.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces CODE, a novel system for quantum entanglement distribution that uses dynamic programming to optimize secure classical information transmission while meeting real-time latency requirements.
AI.motivation: Current entanglement distribution solutions are limited by restrictive assumptions, high computational complexity, and metrics that don't align with practical quantum network needs, particularly for secure classical information transmission.
AI.method: Four key advances: 1) Introduces Ensemble Capacity (EC) metric for secure classical information; 2) Generalized mathematical formulation removing structural restrictions; 3) Dynamic programming-based hypergraph generation algorithm preserving continuous fidelities; 4) CODE system-level orchestration framework with two-tiered architecture.
AI.result: The DP-driven architecture achieves superior private classical information capacity and significant computational complexity reductions, meeting sub-second latency thresholds required for dynamic quantum network operation.
AI.conclusion: CODE provides an efficient, practical solution for entanglement distribution that aligns with real-world quantum network requirements, overcoming limitations of prior approaches through novel metrics, formulations, and optimization algorithms.

title: Analytical Solutions of One-Dimensional ($1\mathcal{D}$) Potentials for Spin-0 Particles via the Feshbach-Villars Formalism
summary: We present a unified analytical and numerical study of the one-dimensional Feshbach--Villars (FV) equation for spin-0 particles in the presence of several representative external potentials. Starting from the FV formulation of the Klein--Gordon equation, we derive the corresponding one-dimensional master equation and analyse its solutions for Coulomb, power-exponential, Cornell, Pöschl--Teller, and Woods--Saxon interactions. For the singular Coulomb and Cornell cases, a Loudon-type cutoff regularisation is implemented on the full line, allowing a mathematically controlled treatment of the origin and an explicit classification of the states by parity. The Coulomb problem exhibits the expected near-degenerate even--odd structure in the cutoff limit, while the Cornell potential combines short-distance Coulomb behaviour with long-distance confinement and produces a finite set of bound states for fixed parameters. The power-exponential potential with $p=1$ is reduced to a Whittaker-type equation and yields an intrinsically relativistic spectrum with no standard Schrödinger bound-state limit in the parameter regime considered. For the smooth short-range Pöschl--Teller and Woods-Saxon potentials, the FV formalism reveals, respectively, the effects of definite parity and spatial asymmetry on the spectrum, wave functions, and particle--antiparticle mixing. In all cases, we reconstruct the full FV spinor, analyse the associated charge density, and compare the relativistic behaviour with the corresponding non-relativistic expectations whenever such a limit exists. The results provide a coherent set of analytical and numerical benchmarks for relativistic scalar bound states in one dimension.

AI.tldr: Analytical and numerical study of 1D Feshbach-Villars equation for spin-0 particles with various external potentials, including Coulomb, power-exponential, Cornell, Pöschl-Teller, and Woods-Saxon potentials, with regularization techniques and comparison to non-relativistic limits.
AI.motivation: To provide a comprehensive study of relativistic scalar bound states in one dimension using the Feshbach-Villars formalism, addressing mathematical challenges of singular potentials and establishing analytical/numerical benchmarks for various interaction types.
AI.method: Derived 1D master equation from FV formulation of Klein-Gordon equation, applied to five representative potentials. Used Loudon-type cutoff regularization for singular Coulomb and Cornell potentials. Reduced power-exponential potential to Whittaker-type equation. Analyzed smooth potentials (Pöschl-Teller, Woods-Saxon) for parity and asymmetry effects. Reconstructed full FV spinors and charge densities.
AI.result: Coulomb potential shows near-degenerate even-odd structure in cutoff limit. Cornell potential yields finite bound states with short-distance Coulomb and long-distance confinement behavior. Power-exponential potential produces intrinsically relativistic spectrum without Schrödinger limit. Pöschl-Teller reveals parity effects, Woods-Saxon shows spatial asymmetry effects on spectrum and particle-antiparticle mixing.
AI.conclusion: The study provides a coherent set of analytical and numerical benchmarks for relativistic scalar bound states in one dimension, demonstrating the FV formalism's capability to handle diverse potential types and offering insights into relativistic versus non-relativistic behavior.

title: A derivation of the late-time volume law for local operator entanglement
summary: Local Operator Entanglement (LOE) has emerged an indicator of quantum chaos in many-body systems. Numerical studies have shown that, in chaotic systems, LOE grows linearly in time and displays a volume-law behavior at late times, scaling proportionally with the number of local degrees of freedom. Despite extensive numerical evidence, complemented by analytical studies in integrable systems, a fully analytical understanding of the emergence of the volume law remains incomplete. In this paper, we contribute toward this goal by deriving a late-time expression for LOE in chaotic systems that exhibits volume-law scaling. Our derivation proceeds by expressing the late-time LOE in the Liouville eigenstate basis and relies on three main assumptions: a higher-order non-resonance condition for the Hamiltonian eigenenergies, the Eigenstate Thermalization Hypothesis (ETH) ansatz for the matrix elements of the initial local operator, and the replacement of Hamiltonian eigenstates with random states in the final expression for LOE. Under these assumptions, we obtain an explicit formula displaying volume-law scaling. Finally, we complement our analytical derivation with numerical simulations of the 1D mixed-field Ising model, testing the resulting formula and exploring the regime of validity of our assumptions.

AI.tldr: Analytical derivation of volume-law scaling for Local Operator Entanglement in chaotic quantum systems using ETH and random state approximations.
AI.motivation: Despite numerical evidence showing Local Operator Entanglement (LOE) grows linearly and exhibits volume-law scaling in chaotic systems, a complete analytical understanding of this phenomenon remains lacking. The paper aims to provide analytical foundations for the observed volume-law behavior.
AI.method: Derives late-time LOE expression in Liouville eigenstate basis using three key assumptions: higher-order non-resonance condition for Hamiltonian eigenenergies, ETH ansatz for initial local operator matrix elements, and replacement of Hamiltonian eigenstates with random states. Validates with numerical simulations of 1D mixed-field Ising model.
AI.result: Obtains explicit analytical formula for LOE displaying volume-law scaling proportional to number of local degrees of freedom. Numerical simulations confirm formula's validity and explore limitations of assumptions.
AI.conclusion: Provides analytical framework explaining volume-law scaling of LOE in chaotic quantum systems, bridging gap between numerical observations and theoretical understanding through combination of ETH, random state approximations, and numerical verification.

title: Quantum Finite Temperature Lanczos Method
summary: The computation of thermal properties of quantum many-body systems is a central challenge in our understanding of quantum mechanics. We introduce the Quantum Finite Temperature Lanczos Method (QFTLM), which extends the finite-temperature Lanczos method to quantum computers by combining real-time quantum Krylov methods with efficient preparation of typical states for trace estimation. This approach enables the computation of thermal expectation values while avoiding the exponential scaling inherent to classical exact simulation techniques. Numerical experiments on the transverse-field Ising model show that QFTLM can reproduce thermal observables over a wide temperature range. We further analyze the influence of Krylov dimension, number of trace-estimator states, and Trotter error, and show that suitable regularization is essential for robustness in noisy settings. These results establish QFTLM as a promising framework for finite-temperature quantum simulation.

AI.tldr: QFTLM extends finite-temperature Lanczos method to quantum computers using real-time quantum Krylov methods and typical state preparation for trace estimation, enabling thermal property computation without exponential classical scaling.
AI.motivation: Computing thermal properties of quantum many-body systems is a fundamental challenge in quantum mechanics, requiring methods that avoid the exponential scaling of classical exact simulation techniques.
AI.method: Quantum Finite Temperature Lanczos Method (QFTLM) combines real-time quantum Krylov methods with efficient preparation of typical states for trace estimation to compute thermal expectation values on quantum computers.
